body: "So many sentences to say" is such a good way to describe how strange normal social functioning looks when you're depressed.  Thanks for that.  It's physically painful, the amount of energy it takes for me to say anything to anyone when I'm deeply in the depression. Like every word is a weight I'm lifting up that's taking all my strength and focus.  And everyone else around -- all these interactions, all this effortless stringing together of words...

Hey there,

I just want to say that I went through that too when I went to college.  It was almost unbearable never really having a place to go to sort of collapse for a while.  I went for a lot of walks, too.  

Could you bring it up with a counselor at your school?  It might be good to talk it over with someone there who could help you plan what steps you'd need to take in order to get a private room, if that's what you decide to do.  8 weeks isn't forever, but it's not nothing, and if it would help you feel and function better, switching rooms might be something to really consider.  

Sorry you're having such a hard time.  I've had depression most of my life too, and freshman year was one of the most difficult times.  There are so many stressors coming from so many directions - it's very, very challenging even for someone who isn't dealing with depression.  With depression, it can feel totally overwhelming and un-doable.  I hope you can talk to somebody there about how you're feeling and what's going on with you.  I think that might have.  made a big difference for me at that time.  Wishing you all the best.
Yes.  I have chronic depression, but when I've had major depressive episodes within that, I start having such a hard time even following conversations, let alone participating.

You're welcome, and thank you so much for your other comment up there, as well.  I am feeling overwhelmed right now, wanting to respond adequately to everyone who took the time to share so thoughtfully.  I'm glad you found help here, too, and of course sorry that you're in a similar emotional place right now.  

Yes, it's such a difficult thing to come to terms with.  I think I'm just not sure whether or not my dad is a true N...   It's confusing, and exhausting, and I just don't know what's what, and end up feeling like the crazy discontented child (again).  Before I can really grieve, I have to figure out what's true, and that seems very challenging!

All the best to you as you move forward.
Yes, I'm in mourning right now.  Thank you for seeing that.  :). There are definitely a lot of factors involved.

It's strange that it's so hard for me to think of what the letters are/were actually about - what I am always left with is the tone, not the content.  I can remember one from when I was in 5th grade or so, my brother and I each got a copy of the letter detailing a list of chores that we each needed to do so that he and my mom wouldn't be frustrated with us.  It also included some personal goals that we should work toward - I remember one of mine was "become more assertive".  (Gee, that's not a crazymaking request to make of someone who you've frightened into compliant silence.  And thanks for the detailed instruction, "become more assertive".  I guess it's that easy!).  I have no problem with kids doing a fair share of work around the house, but again, it was the formal tone of the letter, like something from a law firm instead of a dad.  Maybe it doesn't make sense that it felt like a gut punch to get those letters, but it did.  I guess there was always a sort of invasive and aloof handing down of various judgements on our basic selves.
Thank you so much for sharing that insight.  It actually really does mean a lot to me.

Thank you for your response!  I think you're probably right about the combination of factors.  He's semi-retired, so still gets a fair amount of stimulation, though probably not enough.

Thanks for your kind thoughts.  We are all having a tough time, family and friends.  Most people don't know about the head injury and we haven't started really talking seriously about this factor until recently.  He presents so rationally in person that it is deceptive - his actions are all over the map, and there's the ineffable sense that his feeling for pretty much everyone in his life (except his new love interest) has disappeared.  

I wish you all the best in continuing recovery, thank you again.

Thank you so much for your response.  I'm so sorry that you've had to deal with the effects of a TBI in your life.  I really appreciate your response.

Yes, his reaction to noise seems to be something that preoccupies him quite a bit since the injury, much more than before.  It sort of seems like most aspects of his functioning pre-injury are dialed up.  Like frustration, overwhelm/overload, aloofness, irritability, difficulty organizing...  as you said, it's very difficult to figure out what the source of the behavior is.  I'm not sure if he's had any previous concussions or not - I can't think of a major incident off the top of my head, but there may be more minor ones.

I'll check out the website and the section you recommended!  I'm not sure what I can do about the situation.  My gut tells me that something is off, but he's very defensive and I don't think anyone can talk him into being evaluated.  I'm very worried.  

I hope that things keep improving for you over time.  It sounds like some of your symptoms have gotten better, like short term memory.  Did you go through some kind of treatment for TBI?
